analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in jobs, housing, credit, and public places.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 42 Senate cosponsors including one Republican, the bill never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write sexual orientation and gender identity into the same federal civil rights laws that already ban discrimination by race and sex, and would clarify that 'sex' discrimination includes pregnancy, sex stereotypes, and related grounds. It would cover employment at businesses with 15 or more workers, housing, credit, federally funded programs, public schools and colleges, jury selection, and a broadened list of public accommodations — including stores, online retailers, salons, banks, shelters, and health care providers. It would also bar the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a defense against these protections.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBT people and women. The bill's findings cite surveys showing frequent housing discrimination against same-sex couples, roughly half the homeownership rate for transgender people, about 1 in 5 transgender people experiencing homelessness, and unequal access to credit based on sexual orientation or gender identity. It would give them the same federal recourse in jobs, housing, credit, and public accommodations that people have long had on grounds of race and sex.

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to Title VII employment protections for employers with 15 or more employees, and to federal and government-employee employment law, with the same exceptions that apply to race and sex claims.
Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, addressing documented discrimination in renting, mortgages, and credit.

Expands the definition of public accommodations to include any establishment providing goods, services, or programs — including stores, shopping centers, online retailers, salons, banks, gas stations, food banks, shelters, and health care or legal services — and to transportation services, and bans discrimination in them by sex, sexual orientation, or gender identity.

Bars federal programs and federally assisted activities from discriminating based on the new categories, extends DOJ enforcement authority, and prohibits denying anyone access to restrooms, locker rooms, or dressing rooms consistent with their gender identity.

Clarifies that 'sex' includes sex stereotypes, pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions, and protects people from discrimination based on association with or perceived membership in a protected class; adds the same protections to jury selection.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, landlords, mortgage and credit lenders, and consumer-facing businesses newly covered as public accommodations would face new nondiscrimination obligations and liability. Religious organizations and business owners with religious objections would lose the ability to raise the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a claim or defense against these specific protections.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 shall not provide a claim or defense under any covered provision — removing a legal shield courts had sometimes recognized for religious objectors, including religious schools, charities, and proprietors.
It prohibits denying anyone access to a shared restroom, locker room, or dressing room consistent with their gender identity — the provision that drew the most contested objections.

It extends public-accommodation law beyond physical places to online retailers and service providers, and covers small service establishments such as salons and funeral homes, broadening federal regulation of small businesses.
The employment mandate reaches any employer with 15 or more employees, imposing compliance costs and litigation exposure on small and mid-sized firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For LGBT people and women, the bill addresses discrimination the findings document in housing, credit, and public life, using legal machinery that already exists for race and sex discrimination, so the administrative burden on business is incremental. The sharpest cost falls on religious objectors, who would lose RFRA as a defense in exactly these cases; that tradeoff, not the economic burden, is the core of the opposition. On balance the bill's benefits to a group facing documented discrimination outweigh its compliance costs, though the religion carve-out is a genuine loss for those who relied on it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the Equality Act on July 23, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote for the remainder of the 114th Congress.
The bill attracted 42 Senate cosponsors — 39 Democrats, 2 independents, and 1 Republican.

The bill's provisions would have amended the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Fair Housing Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and federal jury-selection law to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, landlords, lenders, and service providers in states without their own protections kept the legal ability to make decisions based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and religious organizations kept the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense. LGBT people and women remained without explicit federal nondiscrimination protection in these areas.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses and religious objectors kept the status quo

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Angus King and Bernie Sanders
for.role: Independent senators from Maine and Vermont

for.name: Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Was the bill's only Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, took no action on the bill; it received no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Religious-liberty advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, chiefly over its bar on using the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense and its facility-access provisions.

sides.party_line_note: 39 of 44 Senate Democrats and both independents cosponsored; only 1 of 54 Republicans did, and the Republican-led committee took no action.

industries.note: They would face new liability for discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, but the bill would also replace a patchwork of state laws and agency interpretations with one clear federal standard — a concern the bill's own findings cite for employers. Many large employers already operated under such state rules.

The Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act additions would bar rejecting tenants or credit applicants based on sexual orientation or gender identity — conduct the findings say is common and leaves transgender people with about half the homeownership rate of others.
Stores, online retailers, salons, banks, shelters, funeral homes, and health care providers would become public accommodations under federal law, unable to refuse service based on the new categories.

Religious schools, charities, and business owners would lose the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a claim or defense against these specific civil rights protections, the provision that drew the strongest organized opposition.
